    INTERVENOR FLORENCE INDEPENDENT SCHOOL DISTRICT’S INITIAL BRIEF

                                               I.
                                INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY

          Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and the LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA TSC”) filed a joint application to amend their certificate of convenience and

necessity (“CCN”). The applicants plan to construct a new 765 kV single-circuit transmission line

between the 765/345 kV expansion at Oncor’s existing Bell County East Switch, located 5.5 miles

southeast of the City of Temple in Bell County, Texas, and the 765/345 kV expansion of LCRA

TSC’s existing Big Hill 345 kV Substation, located 13 miles northeast of the City of Eldorado in

Schleicher County, Texas.1

          On April 27, 2026, Florence Independent School District timely filed its Motion to

Intervene in the above referenced cause.2 Intervenor Florence Independent School District

(hereinafter “FISD” or “District”), a political subdivision in the state of Texas, submits this its



1
    Applicant ONCOR/LCRA TSC’s Exhibit1
2
    SOAH Order No. 14.

Florence ISD’s Initial Brief                                                                 1
SOAH DKT NO. 473-26-16349/PUC DKT NO. 59475
 Initial Brief in the above-referenced matter. FISD serves students and families in the vicinity of

the proposed routes cited in ONCOR and LCRA TSC’s application. The proposed routes that

include Link F6 and Link F34 would place 765-kV high voltage lines in proximity to Florence

Elementary School (“School”). It is the District’s position that routes that place transmission lines

near the School may pose, among other things, a health risk to students, and transmission lines that

do not include Link F34 and Link F6 would best meet the Commission’s criteria.

                                                      II.

                                                JURISDICTION

           The Commission has jurisdiction over this matter under the Public Utility Regulatory Act

(“PURA”) §§ 14.001, 37.053, 37.054, 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101. The State Office of

Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”) has jurisdiction over this proceeding under Tex. Gov't Code

§ 2003.049 and PURA § 14.053.

                                                         III.

                      ISSUES RELATED TO THE GRANT OF CERTIFICATE

           When approving an application and granting a certificate, the Commission “may approve

an application for a CCN only if the Commission finds that the CCN is necessary for the service,

accommodation, convenience or safety of the public.”3 The Commission shall approve, deny or

modify a request when considering numerous factors in its decision including “community

values.”4

A.         Route Consideration:
           1.      Community Values: Impact on Florence Elementary School




3
    Commission Staff: Direct Testimony of John Poole, pg. 7, Lines 12-15.
4
    PURA §37.056(a)(4).

Florence ISD’s Initial Brief                                                                   2
SOAH DKT NO. 473-26-16349/PUC DKT NO. 59475
         The transmission line should not be placed near Florence Elementary School, a school

“which opened in August of 2025” and “serves approximately 530 students.”5 It is an undisputed

fact that the proposed line will be placed in proximity to the School. The applicant’s routing

witness physically visited the property in June 2025 and confirmed the presence of this facility. 6

It is also not in dispute that Link F34 will run within 520 feet of the elementary school campus.7

Furthermore, it was confirmed in the hearing that the application erroneously identified the School

as a habitable structure, when it should also have been identified as an elementary school. This

indicator has since been corrected by applicants.8

        When considering a proposed route, “routing a transmission line should include

consideration of population centers.” 9 In fact, community values “is not defined in statute or rule,

but the Commission has defined that term as ‘a shared appreciation of an area or other mutual

resource by a national, regional, or local community.’”10 Over 50 individuals, composed of staff,

parents, board members and administrators of Florence ISD have expressed concern over Link F6

and Link F34 near the district’s only elementary school.11 In fact, the avoidance of the placement

of transmission lines near a school facility has been considered and examined by the Commission

and the courts. Among many considerations, the health and safety of the students is paramount for

the analysis. In Houston Lighting & Power Co. v. Klein Independent School District, the Court

addressed a “relatively new scientific concern – the possible health effects or risks associated with

 exposure to high voltage power lines.” 12 The Court determined that the PUC is “required to

consider the safety of the public…” when considering factors for site selection.13 In this case, the

applicant has submitted a set of route selections that may not be considered in the best interest of

the students of the FISD community. Link F6 and Link F34 appear to have been chosen to meet

regulatory requirements only, but the method behind the selection failed to account for the issues

that could arise for the School. In his testimony, the applicant’s routing witness stated the

following:

        “If I can avoid a school, I'm certainly going to look to. However, if there are -- as
        the routing witness, I have to provide a geographically diverse set of routes. And
        then I also have to look at other things in a particular region that may be steering
        the routing of my transmission line alternative. So – so the explanation of, you
        know, how we factor that, we certainly recognize schools and the sensitivities to
        the, you know, public of the schools. But sometimes we have to give that route to
        satisfy the geographic diversity requirement. And, at the same time, we [have] to
        give other alternatives that the Applicant can consider in their evaluation of the
        routes.’14

        The witness further testified that they [Oncor] “coordinate with all the school districts about

the project and help in identifying locations of interest within their district,” however this

interaction did not happen with respect to FISD. The Superintendent of Schools for Florence ISD

indicated in his testimony that meaningful discussions with the applicants did not take place.15 In

fact, Applicant did not reach out to the District at all for a consultation. Considering that Florence

Elementary School is a “cornerstone” of FISD’s “community’s daily life, safety and identity” and

has the “capacity to grow to 740 students as residential development occurs in the area,” a

consultation with the District administration would have been helpful in this process. 16 It has

 already been determined that schools “are obviously valued within a community as a public

resource for education, sporting events, public meetings, recreation etc.”17 In fact, the “route that

avoids such an impact is more consistent with community values than one that does not.”18 Link

F6 and Link F34 should be rejected in favor of routes that maintain greater separation from schools

and nearby residences.

         2.       Habitable Structures: Florence Elementary School

         When a proposed route is considered, there must be consideration regarding the presence

of habitable structures near a proposed location for a transmission line.19 In fact, one “means of

measuring the impact of the proposed transmission line on the community is a consideration of

how close the line is to habitable structures.”20 As stated by a witness for the applicant, they do

not “want to route any components of the school building, playground areas, those types of

locations that would be within the right-of-way.”21 The “Commission defines habitable structures

as those normally inhabited by humans or intended to be inhabited by humans on a daily or regular

basis, including single and multi-family dwellings, apartment buildings, commercial and industrial

structures, businesses, churches, hospitals, and schools.”22 The Florence Elementary School, a

habitable structure, is primarily located near the proposed F34 link.23 Routing the 765-kV line

 along this property would place high-voltage infrastructure in proximity to a school facility and

student activity areas which would undermine the educational environment. Furthermore, the

application of the policy of prudent avoidance includes the “limiting of exposures to electric and

magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.”24 The PUC

has consistently given significant weight to minimizing the number of habitable structures within

the proximity threshold, and route selection decisions frequently turn on which proposed route

affects the fewest habitable structures. It has been acknowledged that “the Commission’s policy

of prudent avoidance is intended to avoid negative consequences.”25 The applicant’s witnesses

have indicated that the health and safety of students and the proximity of the school to the

transmission line was not examined or even researched before the F6/F34 link was selected. After

confirming that the proposed route did run by Florence Elementary School, the applicants’ witness

stated that the team did not consult with the Texas Education Agency or the Department of Health

and Human Services regarding the impact on elementary school students and the proximity to the

transmission line.26 The witness also confirmed that they were not aware of any long-term effects

on the health and safety of elementary school students from transmission lines in proximity to the

campus nor did they consult any studies to that effect.27 Without any kind of assurance from the

applicant on this issue, it is FISD’s position that any such proposed route by a school should be

avoided. “As the need for electrical power increases, so does the need for increased voltage to

transmit that power efficiently. The electrical current flowing through a transmission line generates

an electromagnetic field. The more current that flows through the line, the greater the

 electromagnetic field.”28 The District believes that an alternative route should be chosen that would

not potentially introduce “noise and chemical pollution” and potentially cause “negative effects”

on its students and its staff. 29

                                                       IV.

                                               CONCLUSION

The record demonstrates that routing the 765-kV line on Links F6 and/or F34 would not be in

compliance with PURA §37.056 and could negatively impact the students and staff of Florence

Elementary School. Florence ISD respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges (ALJs)

recommend the rejection of any route that utilizes Link F6 and/or Link F34 due to the potential

adverse impact on the Florence Elementary School and the District community.
